Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn A consortium led by German giant Siemens Mobility was awarded three major contracts to modernize railway signaling and interlocking systems in Romania, worth a total of approximately EUR 308 million, according to Profit.ro . The contracts were awarded by the Romanian railway infrastructure company CFR to the consortium formed by Siemens Mobility, as leader, and the companies Elsitel (Turkey) and IMSAT (Romania). The projects include the modernization of signaling infrastructure on approximately 560 kilometers of railway lines, including 66 stations, 13 centralized operating centers and 122 railway level crossings, and over 2,000 signals. https://albeu.com/english/european-intel.text: lajme kosove maqedoni bota opinion lifestyle shendetesi receta gatimi enciklopedi english sport tech auto livescore REZULTATET ZGJEDHJET 2025 moti në shqipëri moti në kosovë moti në maqedoni travel An investigation by The Telegraph has identified 10 new Kremlin bases equipped with launch platforms for long-range kamikaze drones. Të lidhura None found Some of these installations are already being used in attacks on Ukraine. Their position near the border enables Russian forces to carry out massive airstrikes, taking advantage of the weakening of Kyiv’s air defenses. However, these bases also pose a long-term risk to NATO member states, as they bring them within range of Russia’s advanced attack drones. Experts warn that the rapid advancement of this technology could turn it into a threat to Europe in the event of a conflict. Some of the bases place Russia’s most powerful drones within striking distance of Warsaw. Intelligence officials from Europe and the United States believe that Moscow is considering the possibility of an armed provocation on Polish territory, missile or drone attacks against critical infrastructure, as well as false-flag operations that would be attributed to Ukraine. A NATO representative told The Telegraph that the alliance was “ready to defend every inch of allied territory” and would continue to “increase our readiness to deter and defend against any threat, including from drones.” The investigation, based on leaked documents and satellite photographs, identified at least 59 new launch rails along Russia’s border with Belarus and Ukraine. These are mechanical guidance structures used to launch fixed-wing drones, replacing traditional runways. Some centers were created by adapting military bases and civilian airports, while other platforms were built in rural areas of Russia. An analysis of images by DroneSec, a company specializing in drone intelligence, showed that around 20 of the recently installed rails appeared to be longer. This suggests that they could be used to launch new Russian models with long-range capabilities. Moscow has rapidly modernized its version of the Iranian Shahed drone. New variants with jet engines and high speeds can strike targets nearly 620 miles away. If these models are used from the identified bases, the Polish capital would be within the operational range of Putin’s forces. There is no evidence that Russia is preparing such an attack, but NATO leaders are taking measures to deal with a possible future conflict. The Kremlin claims that even the slower and older versions of the drones could reach the shores of the United Kingdom. However, any attempt to attack Britain from these bases would be very likely to face interception. According to Ukrainian government documents published online, the latest Geran-4 and Geran-5 models are fast enough to evade air-defense systems and can carry payloads of up to 90 kg. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the GUR, has also warned that Russia is equipping Geran drones with air-to-air missiles aimed at striking aircraft defending Kyiv’s airspace. Satellite photographs show a significant increase in capacity for high-tech drones. One of the bases has enough space to hold more than 1,000 drones at the same time. Additional launch rails are also being built at some of the main locations, indicating Moscow’s intention to further expand its offensive drone capabilities. According to The Telegraph, the bases are supplied by several munitions factories scattered throughout Russia. Among them is the Alabuga special economic zone, a Russian drone-production campus that produces 6,000 units a year. Mike Monnik, chief executive and founder of DroneSec, who analyzed the satellite imagery, said that the Kremlin had “significantly expanded” its drone network with the aim of “attacking Ukraine and keeping NATO states at risk of such attacks.” “The expansion of launch sites shows that Russia has increased its ability to launch a greater number of drones, while at the same time using technology that makes the new models more difficult to intercept. These two factors give Russia the ability to use an ever-increasing number of unmanned aerial systems against Ukraine and make it more difficult for Ukrainian forces to neutralize the new Russian models,” he added. A NATO official told The Telegraph that drones “have fundamentally changed the character of modern warfare and have become a decisive factor on the battlefield.” He stressed that the alliance “is rapidly expanding our ability to produce, operate and neutralize drones on a large scale.” The investigation documents the rapid growth of Russia’s drone capabilities and raises concerns about Putin’s ambition to create new threats to NATO allies. Open-source tracking data shows that seven of the 10 locations identified by The Telegraph have been used during some of Moscow’s most recent bombardments of Kyiv. https://www.lgbtqnation.com/2026/10/homo.text: An unintended confluence of AI, blind allegiance, and rabid homophobia is landing supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin's anti-LGBTQ+ crusade in court, leading even his most faithful supporters to question the authoritarian state's methods. Homophobic authors of anti-LGBTQ+ posts are now regularly being charged under the very same laws meant to suppress the LGBTQ+ community in Russia, Mediazona reports. A raft of cases is arriving in front of magistrates accusing fans of the Russian Supreme Court's 2023 decision outlawing the “LGBT movement” — and the total ban on so-called LGBTQ+ symbols that came with it — of violating the law. One woman dragged before a judge, called the ban the "right decision" when it was proposed. She posted rainbows and other images in support of the ban, saying she was "fiercely against this filth." Her offending post on the Russian social media platform VK came with the sarcastic hashtag #YourFavoriteUnicorn, and a photo captioned, “Welcome to the LGBT kindergarten! Who is QUEER? Maybe I should join LGBT too? Lesbians are so cool! Let’s draw a rainbow!” She was fined 1,500 rubles, or about $18. A man fined a similar amount and sentenced to a day in jail pointed to AI as the culprit. “I reposted a picture where Zelensky, Macron, and several other European leaders are shown with a fascist swastika and a rainbow. The FSB’s AI decided I was spreading propaganda,” he said, referring to the Russian security service. “In court, I asked the judge about patriotic films where actors do the Nazi salute and wear swastikas on their sleeves without being sent to prison,” the man said. “But they locked me up for a day, explaining that I considered Zelensky and Macron to be fascist and gay, which is openly advertised in the media. I asked if I should officially apologize to Zelensky. In short, the AI that reads our messages is a complete moron, and we mean nothing to it.” Judges in the cases, as well as authorities summoning the violators to court, appear to be abandoning any discretion they might have and are following the letter of the draconian law, regardless of the violators' intent. “I created a video criticizing LGBT, but [the police officer] took screenshots and sent them without explanation," said one man who regularly employs the slur evropediki, or "Eurof**s," in his posts. "The court didn’t bother to figure it out and fined me.” The judge didn't get his brand of humor, he complained. In St. Petersburg, a court targeted the author of a poem titled “It’s Cool to Be Gay" posted to socials, despite its anti-LGBTQ+ message. “Let’s hit balls / Like billiard players / But we aren’t athletes / We are homo-mast**bators,” one verse read. And in Moscow, a resident was fined 100,000 rubles (about $1,240) for posting a video that attacked Nazis as debaucherous and gay, showing a young man shaving his head, putting on skinhead clothing, and having sex with two similar-looking men. It ended with a swastika and the phrase, “Join our ranks!!!” The court ruled it was “LGBT propaganda.” With the Russian government's dual attacks on LGBTQ+ identity — both the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling and the country's anti-LGBTQ+ propaganda laws, initiated in 2013 and expanded in 2022 — social media, books, films, television series, and advertising are subject to total censorship. Dozens of individuals are facing criminal charges under the laws, while administrative cases for “propaganda” or “extremist symbols” run into the hundreds. Russian LGBTQ+ organizations are being dismantled and their staffs threatened. Even a homophobic priest in the country, where the Russian Orthodox Church is a staunch supporter of Putin's self-declared war on "Western degeneracy," has been the victim of his own hatred. The Polish native, a resident in Russia for nearly 25 years, posted a photo of the leader of the Moscow Catholic Archdiocese, whom he's accused of supporting the LGBTQ+ community, next to a rainbow flag to “attract attention.” He's been deported back to Poland and banned from Russia.
